extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and professional screenwriters / narrative writers studying story design
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing cinematic stories: how to create meaning, protagonist-driven structure, levels of conflict, the narrative 'gap', and stakes/risk that compel audience empathy and closure.

rubrics_metrics.name: No endings by random chance
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that end by random chance, doubly charged or not, are meaningless, not ironic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An ending that relies on chance robs the story of meaning. Avoid resolutions that occur through random events rather than through the protagonist's embodied choices and the story's causal logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate mixed-valence climaxes
rubrics_metrics.description: If at climax the life situation of the protagonist is both positive and negative, express it so that the two charges remain separated in the audience's experience and don't cancel each other out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an ending contains both gains and losses, structure and present them so the audience feels each charge distinctly (else the meaning dissolves). Avoid muddled climaxes where opposing emotional outcomes neutralize each other, leaving the audience unsure what the story stands for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect your Controlling Idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Once you discover your Controlling Idea, respect it. Never allow yourself the luxury of thinking, 'It's just entertainment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat your Controlling Idea as the organizing truth of the story. Every scene and choice should serve that idea rather than treating the story as mere diversion. The Controlling Idea should inform theme, character actions, and climax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extract Controlling Idea from the climax and believe it
rubrics_metrics.description: Study your Story Climax and extract from it your Controlling Idea. Ask yourself: Is this the truth? Do I believe in the meaning of my story? If the answer is no, toss it and start again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author must personally believe the Controlling Idea. If you don't accept the story's core truth, the work lacks conviction. Only proceed to promote/publish a story when you can answer 'yes' to this test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stories convey ideas through emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: All coherent tales express an idea veiled inside an emotional spell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that stories persuade by feeling, not by overt rational argument. Even entertainment transmits an idea; be conscious of what idea your emotional storytelling conveys and the social consequences of that idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artist's social responsibility: tell the truth
rubrics_metrics.description: We have only one responsibility: to tell the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author should not self-censor to avoid uncomfortable truths. In service of truth, even unpleasant or morally repellent ideas may be expressed; oppose censorship and trust the marketplace of ideas. Moral outrage at content does not negate its artistic validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance of story is intangible energy, not language
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer's raw material is not language; language is merely a medium. At the nucleus of a story is an intangible 'substance'—an energy that compels audience response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach story from the inside-out: inhabit your protagonist and craft scenes that transmit this intangible energy. Don't mistake clever prose for story substance; prioritize dramatic causality, desire, conflict, and emotional impact over purely literary ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist must be willful
rubrics_metrics.description: A PROTAGONIST is a willful character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The protagonist must possess willpower that drives action. Will can be subtle or hidden beneath passive behavior, but avoid protagonists who lack desire and agency; a truly passive protagonist cannot sustain story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist must have a conscious desire
rubrics_metrics.description: The PROTAGONIST has a conscious desire: a need or goal and can answer 'What do you want?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give the protagonist a clear, articulable object of desire (external or internal). Even if the desire evolves, the character must exhibit a conscious aim that motivates choices and propels plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist may have an unconscious contradictory desire
rubrics_metrics.description: The most memorable protagonists tend to have not only a conscious but an unconscious desire; the two contradict each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Layer character with an unconscious need that conflicts with the conscious goal to create inner tension and complexity. The audience senses this contradiction and finds the character compelling; avoid characters whose inner life is one-dimensional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist must have capacities to pursue the desire convincingly
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist's characterization must be appropriate: believable combination of qualities to pursue his desires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the character has the skills, resources, temperament, or circumstances that make their pursuit plausible—even if they ultimately fail. Implausible capabilities break audience belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist must have at least a chance to attain the desire
rubrics_metrics.description: The PROTAGONIST must have at least a chance to attain his desire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the protagonist has no realistic possibility of fulfillment, the audience will disengage. Maintain hope (hypothetical possibility) so viewers remain invested, even when odds are long.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist must pursue to the human limit; the story must reach a final action
rubrics_metrics.description: The PROTAGONIST has the will and capacity to pursue the object of desire to the end of the line (the human limit established by setting and genre). A STORY must build to a final action beyond which the audience cannot imagine another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories should escalate to an irreversible climax that resolves the central tension and provides closure; avoid endings that leave audiences inventing missing scenes or unresolved contingencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist must be empathetic (not necessarily sympathetic)
rubrics_metrics.description: The PROTAGONIST must be empathetic; he may or may not be sympathetic (likable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empathy means the audience recognizes 'like me' in the character; sympathy (likability) is optional. You can make an unlikable character empathetic by revealing inner truth (conscience, conflict). Lack of empathy breaks the audience-story bond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience bond is formed by empathy
rubrics_metrics.description: The audience's emotional involvement is held by the glue of empathy. If the writer fails to fuse a bond between filmgoer and protagonist, we sit outside feeling nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design your protagonist and scenes to create moments of identification (shared humanity, conscience, inner conflict) so the audience 'roots for' the character. Avoid hypocrisy or dispassionate portrayal that leads to audience rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters act conservatively from their point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: All characters, in the pursuit of desire at any moment, will always take the minimum, conservative action from their point of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make actions believable by reflecting the character's subjective calculus of minimal risk/reward. Use this principle to justify character choices; apparent extreme behavior must be defensible from that character's POV.

rubrics_metrics.name: In story, action must provoke antagonism (the Gap principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: In story we concentrate on moments in which a character takes an action expecting a useful reaction but instead the world reacts differently or more powerfully—provoking antagonism and opening a 'gap' between expectation and result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus scenes on these ruptures (the Gap) where probability meets necessity; they generate dramatic conflict. Avoid scenes where expected enabling reactions simply occur as they would in mundane life.

rubrics_metrics.name: World of a character: three concentric levels of conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: The character's world consists of concentric circles of antagonism: (1) innermost self (mind, body, emotion), (2) personal relationships (intimacy beyond social role), and (3) extra-personal world (institutions, other individuals, environment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three levels to source obstacles and escalate conflict. Antagonism can arise from within, between people close to the protagonist, or from social/natural forces and institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story is born where subjective expectation collides with objective necessity (the Gap)
rubrics_metrics.description: STORY is born in that place where the subjective and objective realms touch: the protagonist's action, taken under a sense of probability, meets necessity—the actual reaction—which creates a gap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design narrative around this collision: the protagonist's minimal action produces an unforeseen but necessary reaction that blocks desire and forces escalation. The Gap creates the need for riskier, costlier subsequent choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity vs. probability: use the discovery of necessity to create truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Every human acts on a sense of probability; only when acting do we discover necessity—the absolute truth of what actually happens. When objective necessity contradicts probability, the fictional gap opens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit the revelation of necessity to transform character and story direction. Scenes should reveal truth through action, not exposition of expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk: every story must establish what the protagonist stands to lose
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask: What is the risk? What's the worst thing that will happen if the protagonist does not achieve his desire? If failure just returns life to normal, the story is misconceived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make stakes meaningful and proportional to the value of the desire. The greater the value, the greater the risk the protagonist must be willing to take (time, money, relationships, life, soul). Use this test to assess whether the story's central pursuit is worth telling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of desire's value is proportional to risk taken
rubrics_metrics.description: The measure of the value of a character's desire is in direct proportion to the risk he's willing to take to achieve it; the greater the value, the greater the risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that protagonists are willing to risk things that align with the story's thematic stakes. This principle applies to writers themselves as creators: meaningful artistic ambition entails real personal risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plural-Protagonist vs. Multiprotagonist design
rubrics_metrics.description: Plural-Protagonist: a group can be a protagonist if (1) all individuals share the same desire and (2) in pursuing it they mutually suffer and benefit. Multiprotagonist: characters pursue separate, independent desires leading to Multiplot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose group-protagonist structures only when members' motivations and fates are communal (Plural-Protagonist). Use Multiprotagonist/Multiplot to portray societies or linked smaller stories, but manage coherence differently than single-protagonist designs.
